Who we are

A community for the whole neighbourhood

Faithful Commons began in 1962 as a handful of families meeting in a front room. Today we are several hundred neighbours of every age who share a building, a weekly rhythm and a commitment to look after one another.

We hold our beliefs with conviction and our questions with honesty. Whether you have belonged to a faith community all your life or have never set foot in one, you will find people here who are glad you came.

pages.title: Our Story
pages.content:
Faithful Commons began in 1962, when four families started meeting in a front room on Linden Street to sing, read and share a meal. They outgrew the room within a year, then a borrowed school hall, and in 1971 they built the stone hall and sanctuary we still use today.

What matters to us

Welcome

Everyone belongs here before they believe anything. We would rather have an honest question than a polite pretence.

Rhythm

We gather, we rest and we serve, week after week. Small faithful habits shape us more than big moments.

Neighbourliness

Our building belongs to the street. The pantry, the suppers and the garden are open to everyone.

Who leads

A council of nine members, elected every two years, looks after the life of the community, and a small staff team of three keeps the building, the pantry and the calendar running. Every gathering is led by a different member of the community.

We do not have all the answers. We do have soup, and a chair, and time to listen.

A long-time member
Plan your first visit

pages.title: Plan Your Visit
pages.content:
Visiting somewhere new for the first time can feel daunting. Here is everything we wish someone had told us before our first Sunday.

What to expect

  • A friendly welcome at the door, and nobody will single you out.
  • About an hour of songs, a short reflection and time to share news.
  • Tea, coffee and something baked afterwards in the hall.
  • Clothes: whatever you are comfortable in.

Finding us

We are at 24 Linden Street, five minutes from the station. The side entrance on Orchard Lane has step-free access, and there is a hearing loop in the sanctuary.

Bicycle racks are by the garden gate; on-street parking is free on Sundays.

Common questions

Do I have to believe anything to come?

No. You are welcome to come, listen, ask questions and make up your own mind.

Are children welcome?

Very. Children can stay with you or join the children's corner, and nobody minds a bit of noise.

Will I be asked for money?

No. A collection box sits by the door for anyone who wishes to give, and that is all.

pages.title: Get Involved
pages.content:
There is a place here for your time and your gifts, whether you can offer an hour a year or an afternoon every week.

Food pantry

Sort, shelve and welcome guests on Saturday mornings.

Open Supper

Cook, set tables or wash up on a Wednesday evening.

Garden crew

Grow vegetables for the pantry alongside the youth group.

How to start

  1. Choose a role that fits your week.
  2. Tell us through the contact page, or catch someone wearing a gold lanyard.
  3. Join a buddy for your first session. That is it.

Volunteers who work with children or vulnerable adults complete a short safeguarding course, which we arrange and pay for.

Say hello

pages.content:

For the Harvest Supper, just let us know how many are coming and any dietary needs. A short message is plenty.

posts.title: Making Room at the Table
posts.excerpt: Hospitality is less about a perfect meal and more about pulling up one more chair. Notes from Sunday's gathering.
posts.content:
On Sunday we talked about tables: the kitchen table where homework gets done, the folding tables in our hall on supper nights, and the small café tables where people finally say the thing they have been carrying for weeks.

Hospitality is easy to confuse with entertaining. Entertaining asks whether the house is tidy enough and the food impressive enough. Hospitality asks a simpler question: is there room for one more?

Three small habits

  1. Notice who is standing. At every gathering someone is hovering at the edge. Invite them to sit.
  2. Learn one name a week. Write it down if you need to. Use it next time.
  3. Keep a spare chair. Literally or otherwise, leave space in your week for an unexpected guest.

The table does not need to be bigger. It needs to be shared.

From Sunday's gathering

This week, try one of the habits above and tell us how it went at Wednesday's open supper. There will, of course, be a seat saved for you.

comments.author: Marion
comments.content: The spare chair idea stayed with me all week. We had three unexpected guests on Friday and nobody felt like an afterthought.

comments.author: Theo
comments.content: Learning one name a week is a habit I can actually keep. Thank you.

posts.title: The Autumn Food Drive Starts This Week
posts.excerpt: From Monday the collection crates are back in the porch. Here is what the pantry needs most and how to help sort on Saturday.
posts.content:
Our neighbourhood pantry feeds around ninety households every week, and the weeks before winter are always the busiest. From Monday, the wooden collection crates are back in the porch and will stay there until the end of November.

What the pantry needs most

  • Tinned fish and beans
  • Rice, pasta and oats
  • Cooking oil
  • Tea and coffee
  • Nappies in sizes 4 and 5
  • Soap and toothpaste
  • Warm socks and gloves
  • Long-life milk

Please check dates before you donate: we cannot give out anything past its best-before date, and sorting expired items takes volunteers away from the people we are here to serve.

Sorting Saturdays

Every Saturday morning from 9:00 to 11:30 we sort, weigh and shelve what has come in. No experience is needed, children are welcome with an adult, and there is always tea. Just come to the side door of the hall.

comments.author: Nadia
comments.content: Dropped off two bags this morning. The crates are already filling up!

posts.title: Notes from Sunday: Rest Is Not a Reward
posts.excerpt: We often treat rest as something to earn once the list is done. What if it is where the week begins instead of where it ends?
posts.content:
Most of us were taught, quietly, that rest is a reward. Finish the work, clear the inbox, tidy the kitchen, and then, maybe, sit down. The list never ends, so neither does the waiting.

On Sunday we wondered aloud what would change if rest came first: if the week began with a pause instead of ending with exhaustion.

Practising a pause

  • Begin one meal a day without a screen at the table.
  • Take a ten-minute walk with no destination and no headphones.
  • Name three things you are grateful for before you sleep.

None of these will fix a hard week. But they are small doors into a different way of living, and we would love to hear which ones you try. Our Quiet Mornings hour on Thursdays is open to anyone who wants to practise together.

comments.author: Ruth
comments.content: The walk without headphones was harder than I expected, and better than I expected.

posts.title: Meet the Choir That Anyone Can Join
posts.excerpt: No auditions, no sheet music required, and nobody minds a wrong note. Inside the Thursday evening community choir.
posts.content:
Every Thursday at half past seven, around thirty people gather in the hall with mugs of tea and sing. Some have sung all their lives. Some had not sung a note since school until a friend dragged them along.

The choir has one rule: there are no auditions. Songs are taught by ear, harmonies are learned in small groups, and the director is famous for saying that a confident wrong note is better than a timid right one.

I came for one week to keep my neighbour company. That was four years ago.

A tenor who never planned to be a tenor

What we sing

Folk songs from around the world, gospel and spirituals, a few rounds and, every December, the carols the whole neighbourhood seems to know. The choir sings at Sunday gatherings once a month and at the Harvest Supper.

Come and listen first

You are welcome to sit in on a rehearsal before joining. Bring a friend, bring a mug, and stay for the last song.

posts.title: Harvest Supper: An Evening for the Whole Neighbourhood
posts.excerpt: Long tables, soup made from the garden, the choir and a ceilidh band. Everyone is welcome and the meal is free.
posts.content:
Our Harvest Supper is the one night of the year when the hall is too small and nobody minds. Saturday 14 November, from six o'clock, the long tables go up and the soup pots come out.

The meal is free and there is no need to book, although it helps the kitchen team if you let us know you are coming. Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options are always on the table.

Bring something to share

If you would like to contribute, bring a dessert, a jar of something you made this summer, or a story about this year's harvest. Every year someone brings a cake that becomes a legend.

Tell us you are coming

comments.author: Ines
comments.content: Our family has not missed one of these in six years. The crumble alone is worth it.

comments.author: Samuel
comments.content: Can we bring a guitar for the ceilidh?

posts.title: Five Ways to Volunteer This Season
posts.excerpt: Not everyone can give a whole Saturday. Here are five ways to serve, from one hour a month to a weekly commitment.
posts.content:
Every autumn we ask the same question: how can more people share in the work without anyone burning out? The answer is usually smaller roles, shared well.

  1. Welcome team. Greet people at the door on Sundays, once a month.
  2. Pantry sorting. Saturday mornings, as often or as rarely as you like.
  3. Supper cooks. Join a kitchen team for one Wednesday each term.
  4. Lifts and errands. Drive a neighbour to an appointment or pick up a prescription.
  5. Garden crew. Weed, water and harvest with the youth group.

Every role comes with a buddy for your first time, and none of them require you to share our beliefs. Neighbours of every faith and none serve alongside us.

We are not looking for heroes. We are looking for people who will show up for an hour.

The volunteer coordinators

If one of these sounds like you, visit the Get Involved page or simply catch someone in a gold lanyard after a gathering.

Get involved

posts.title: Quiet Mornings: A New Midweek Prayer Hour
posts.excerpt: From October, the sanctuary is open every Thursday from seven to eight for silence, candles and a short reading.
posts.content:
Many of you asked for a quieter space in the middle of the week, so from the first Thursday of October the sanctuary will be open from seven until eight in the morning.

There is no programme. The candles will be lit, the heating will be on, and at half past seven someone will read a short passage of poetry or prose, followed by more silence. Come for five minutes or the full hour.

A few gentle guidelines

  • Arrive and leave whenever you like.
  • Phones on silent, please.
  • Tea is served in the porch afterwards for anyone who wants to talk.

Quiet Mornings are open to everyone, whatever you believe or are still working out.

comments.author: Agnes
comments.content: This has become the anchor of my week. Thank you to whoever lights the candles so early.

posts.title: What the Youth Group Learned Building a Garden
posts.excerpt: Eight raised beds, one stubborn compost heap and a summer of teamwork. The youth group on what the garden taught them.
posts.content:
In April, the patch of grass behind the hall was just that: a patch of grass. By September it held eight raised beds, a compost heap, a bench built from reclaimed timber and enough courgettes to feed half the street.

The youth group, aged eleven to sixteen, planned, built and tended it themselves, with a little help from a retired carpenter and a lot of watering cans.

In their own words

You cannot rush a tomato. I tried.

Age 13

The best part was giving the vegetables to the pantry and seeing them go home with people.

Age 15

What grew

  • Courgettes, far too many
  • Runner beans
  • Three kinds of tomato
  • Sunflowers taller than the leaders

Next spring the group plans to add a herb spiral and a small pond. If you have spare tools, seeds or an afternoon, they would love the help.

comments.author: Daniel
comments.content: So proud of these young people. The courgette soup at harvest supper came straight from their beds!
